title: Four ultimate realities
hookLine: consciousness, mental factors, matter, and nibbana
carry: three realities pass; nibbana alone is unmade

lines: HOW MANY THINGS IN THIS ROOM?
cards: How many things are in the room you're sitting in? Count the ordinary way and you'll never finish: a lamp, a cable, a sock under the couch, a spider in the corner, the smell of coffee, a worry about Thursday.
The Abhidhamma counts the ultimate way, and its answer is short. However crowded the room, however crowded the mind, everything real in that sense falls into four kinds. Four drawers.

teach.b: Today's word is paramattha, usually put into English as ultimate, or the highest sense: what the Abhidhamma counts as real when everything is taken apart, the bottom of the analysis, where taking apart stops.
The manuals name four. The first drawer is citta, consciousness: the bare knowing of something. Seeing a color, hearing a sound, knowing a thought.
The second is cetasika, the mental factors that come along with each moment of knowing and color it: feeling pleasant or unpleasant, attention, greed, kindness, doubt.

The two always arrive together, the way light and the color of a stained glass window arrive together. The third is rupa, matter: the body, and the physical world the senses meet. Hardness, warmth, movement, color, sound.
Everything in those three drawers arises from conditions, stays a moment, and passes away. Nothing in them lasts. The fourth drawer is different.
It's nibbana, the ending of craving that this path has met before. The manuals list it as the one reality not made from conditions. It doesn't arise and doesn't pass away.
In a discourse in the Udana, the Buddha speaks, in paraphrase, of something unborn and unmade, and says that if there weren't, there'd be no escape from what is born and made.
Notice what isn't in any drawer. No lamp. No sock.
And no self, sitting behind it all as the owner. A person, in the ultimate way of speaking, is the first three drawers, moving fast, and the fourth is what the whole path points toward.

how: Students of the Abhidhamma in Theravada communities learn the four ultimate realities, consciousness, mental factors, matter and nibbana, as the opening frame of the manuals they study.

o: a perfect teacher who has nothing left to learn
the highest heaven, where the gods live longest
what counts as real once everything is taken apart

p: the mental factors that color it
matter, the body and the world

s: in the ultimate sense, a lamp is one of the four realities
a lamp is the ordinary way of speaking. the four are consciousness, mental factors, matter and nibbana.
nibbana is counted as one of the four realities
the fourth drawer: the one reality the manuals list as not made from conditions.
the manuals find a self behind the four realities
no drawer holds a self as the owner of it all.

games.q: a moment of worry about Thursday turns up while you sit. you're sorting it the Abhidhamma way. where does the worry itself, the anxious flavor, go?
games.why: the knowing of the thought is citta; the worry that colors it is a mental factor, a cetasika. the tight chest that comes with it would be rupa.

practice: If you'd like, wait for one moment to stand out, a sound, an itch, a thought about later, and sort it gently: the knowing of it is the first drawer; the flavor that came with it, liking, impatience, curiosity, is the second; the sound or the skin is the third.
The fourth you can't put a moment into, so let it rest in the background as what the sorting is for. Don't worry about getting it right; just sort the next moment the same way.

wordCard.voice: Paramattha. Ultimate reality, in the Abhidhamma's sense: consciousness, mental factors, matter, and nibbana. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: the ultimate, or highest, sense: what the Abhidhamma counts as real when everything is taken apart.

carryVoice: Your line: three realities pass; nibbana alone is unmade. Tomorrow, the first drawer opens wide.

sources.ref: Abhidhammattha Sangaha I.2 (the four ultimate realities)
